title: Homework: how much is any use?

turns.speaker: Tess
turns.text: The primary school's dropped homework entirely. Reading together, and that's it.

turns.speaker: Omar
turns.text: Half the parents will be furious and half will be quietly relieved.

turns.speaker: Fiona
turns.text: The evidence at primary age is genuinely weak, though. The correlation with attainment is close to nothing until about thirteen.

turns.speaker: Fiona
turns.text: In secondary, yes, up to a point. Somewhere past ninety minutes a night it goes flat and then negative.

turns.speaker: Omar
turns.text: What worries me isn't the average, it's the spread. Homework is the part of school that happens at home, so it measures the home.

turns.speaker: Tess
turns.text: A quiet room, a desk, a parent who can explain a fraction.

turns.speaker: Omar
turns.text: Exactly. Two children do the same worksheet in completely different conditions and we grade it as if it were the same task.

turns.speaker: Fiona
turns.text: Which is the argument for homework clubs rather than for abolition.

turns.speaker: Omar
turns.text: Agreed, although those need staff who are already doing too much.

turns.speaker: Tess
turns.text: There's a defence nobody's made yet, which is that it teaches you to work when nobody's watching. That's a real skill.

turns.speaker: Fiona
turns.text: It is, and you could teach it deliberately in twenty minutes a week rather than as a side effect of four hours of it.

turns.speaker: Tess
turns.text: That would require admitting what it was for, mind you.

points: A primary school has abolished homework except shared reading.
Fiona says evidence for homework at primary age is weak, with little correlation to attainment before about thirteen.
In secondary school the effect is positive up to roughly ninety minutes a night, then flattens and reverses.
Omar's objection concerns inequality: homework happens at home, so it measures home conditions rather than the pupil.
Fiona argues this supports homework clubs rather than abolition, though staffing is a constraint.
Tess defends homework as teaching independent work, which Fiona says could be taught deliberately in far less time.
